title: Akyeke
author: Nzema tradition
desc: Grated cassava fermented five to seven days to pH 3.21, washed, dewatered, sifted, sun-dried and steamed — a documented process rather than a household recipe.
longDesc: Akyeke is the Nzema fermented cassava staple of Ghana's Western Region, the same dish as Ivorian attiéké. It is published here as a documented process rather than a recipe, because the research literature gives the fermentation properly but no named source gives home quantities. Grated cassava ferments five to seven days with an inoculum; water is added several times to wash out starch and colour; the mash is dewatered, sifted and sun-dried, then steamed. The cues are real: the texture breaks down to smooth and non-rubbery, the pH falls from 5.15 to 3.21, and titratable acidity rises to between about 1.1 and 1.7 per cent.
ingredients: An inoculum — a portion of previously fermented cassava mash
// Quantities are not published in any named source. See the note.
steps: Mix with an inoculum of previously fermented mash.
During fermentation the texture breaks down from rubbery to smooth and non-rubbery.
Add water several times during the ferment to wash out some of the starch and colour.
Dewater the fermented mash under pressure.
Sift the dewatered mash to granules.
Sun-dry — about an hour, in the one source that times it.
// FERMENTATION ENDPOINT: pH should fall from about 5.15 to about 3.21, with titratable acidity rising to roughly 1.1-1.7 per cent as lactic acid.
chefTips: The texture cue is the one a cook can actually use: during fermentation the cassava dough breaks down from rubbery to smooth and non-rubbery. That change is the endpoint.
pH falls from about 5.15 to about 3.21 over five to seven days. If you have pH strips, that is the definitive test.
The repeated washing during fermentation is not optional — it removes starch and colour and it is part of what makes akyeke white and light rather than grey and dense.
An inoculum of previously fermented mash is specified in the research. Starting from nothing will work but takes longer and is less predictable.

Raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds. The long fermentation, the repeated washing, the drying and the final steaming all reduce them — this is a safety process as much as a flavour one, and none of the steps should be skipped.
Two papers disagree sharply on duration: five to seven days in the traditional survey, twelve hours for an inoculum-prepared convenience product. They are measuring different things.
This is published as a process, not a recipe. No named source gives household quantities, and none has been invented.
commonMistakes: Cutting the fermentation short of the texture change.
Omitting the final steaming, which is a safety step as well as a cooking one.
Treating the twelve-hour figure from the convenience-product paper as the traditional time.
Expecting household quantities, which do not exist in the literature.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE, and that distinction is the point of this entry. The fermentation is well documented in the Ghanaian research literature with real endpoints; NO NAMED SOURCE PUBLISHES HOME QUANTITIES. None have been invented. The ingredient list carries a header saying so.

PRIMARY SOURCE: Obilie M.E., 'Microbiological and Biochemical Changes in the Production of Akyeke – A Fermented Cassava product', MPhil thesis, Department of Nutrition and Food Science, University of Ghana, 2001, advisors Tano-Debrah K. and Amoa-Awua W.

PROCESS, verbatim: 'Fermenting grated cassava for 5-7 days with an inoculum, water is added several times to remove some amount of starch and colour from the fermented cassava mash, dewatered, sifted and sun dried before steaming.'

THE CUES, all verbatim, and the reason this fermentation clears the bar where several others in this collection do not. TEXTURE: 'During fermentation, a breakdown of the texture of cassava dough occurs to give a smooth and non-rubbery texture.' pH: 'pH dropped from 5.15 to 3.21 after fermentation.' ACIDITY: 'Titratable acidity expressed as lactic acid increased from 0.38%-0.32% to 1.67%-1.11% after fermentation for field and laboratory samples respectively.' That is a time, an observable texture change, and two measurable endpoints.

A SECOND PAPER WITH A VERY DIFFERENT DURATION: Amofa B., Manu F.D., Oduro I., 'Development of Convenient Akyeke', ICAST 2015, KNUST Department of Food Science and Technology. As printed: 'Freshly milled cassava… pressed and fermented for 12 hours… sieved and steamed.' For the inoculum-prepared sample it gives 'pH of 3.5 and TTA of 0.72%'.

DISAGREEMENT, UNRECONCILED AND NOT AVERAGED: Obilie (2001) gives 5-7 days with a final pH of 3.21. Amofa et al. (2015) give 12 HOURS, with pH 3.5 for the inoculated sample only. The two papers are measuring different things — field and laboratory samples of the traditional product against a deliberately engineered convenience product — and no choice is made between them. A reader following the twelve-hour figure is making a different product.

A THIRD SOURCE, with no fermentation data: 'Akyeke, the Nzema delicacy gaining popularity across Ghana', Ghana News Agency, dateline 'Takoradi, April 09, GNA'. Its steps are grate and ferment cassava, drain, sun dry 'close to an hour', steam. It gives NO fermentation duration and NO cue. The sun-drying time above comes from this source.

ON THE NAME: a Wikipedia pointer for 'nhyira/akyeke' was checked and the sources name only akyeke. 'Nhyira' returned no dish — it is a Twi word for blessing in other contexts and no source treats it as a food. See also the gaps note: nhyira is recorded as an empty dish name rather than a synonym.
ON THE CROSS-BORDER IDENTITY: the same product is attiéké in Côte d'Ivoire, where it is far better known. The Nzema of Ghana's Western Region make it on their side of the border.

THE SAFETY POINT, which no single source states in full but which follows from the documented process: raw cassava carries cyanogenic glycosides, and the long fermentation, repeated washing, dewatering, drying and steaming together are what reduce them. The tips note this; it is assembled from the process description rather than quoted, and is labelled accordingly.
storage: Dried granules keep months in a sealed container. Steamed akyeke should be eaten the same day.
healthBenefits: Fermentation raises the B-vitamin content and reduces antinutrients.
The lactic acid bacteria involved are the same families used in other fermented staples.
The process substantially reduces cassava's cyanogenic compounds.
culturalNote: Akyeke belongs to the Nzema in Ghana's far southwest, on the border with Côte d'Ivoire, where the same food is attiéké and is eaten by millions. That the Ghanaian version is documented mainly in university theses rather than cookbooks says something about whose foods get written down — the research is excellent and the home recipe does not exist in print.
